extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and patent examiners handling PCT international applications (unity of invention assessment)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing unity of invention (Rule 13 / Rule 13.2) at the international search stage: when claimed alternatives may be treated as a single invention or must be split into separate inventions (and when additional search fees are invited). Includes examples and minimum-reasoning guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (a priori): common property/activity plus significant structural element
rubrics_metrics.description: A group of alternatives meets the requirement of unity of invention (a priori) if the alternatives have a common property or activity and share a significant structural element that is essential to the common property or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: SEQ ID NOs sharing an element that allows a probe to detect disease-specific mRNA; compounds sharing the iminothioether group linked to a six-atom ring and the same therapeutic use. Some Offices may regard such a claim as a Markush grouping when both requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity (a posteriori): shared technical feature must contribute over prior art (Rule 13.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A shared or corresponding technical feature that links claimed alternatives must define a contribution over the prior art; if the shared feature is known in the prior art it is not a 'special technical feature' and cannot establish unity a posteriori.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nucleic acids that contain a conserved motif known in prior art lack unity a posteriori because the shared motif does not form the contribution of the group as a whole. The presence of prior art can change groupings and whether separate inventions exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markush grouping acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: A Markush-style claim (listing alternatives) can be acceptable when the alternatives share a common property/activity and either share a common structure or belong to a recognized class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Catalyst example: (X) and (X+a) share a common component and catalytic activity so a Markush grouping is acceptable. Offices differ; some may still treat as a Markush grouping even for biological molecules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognized class requirement for alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives included in a group must be members of a 'recognized class' of compounds (a class already known from the prior art that a skilled addressee would expect to behave in the same way) for unity to be accepted on that basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Herbicidal composition example: listing many chemically diverse substances (inorganic salts, amides, nitriles, phenols, heterocyclics) does not form a recognized class and thus lacks unity. Recognized class examples: TNF inhibitors, serine/threonine kinases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common source alone is insufficient for unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely deriving claimed biological molecules from the same source (e.g., human liver) is not sufficient to meet unity requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polynucleotide example: SEQ ID NOs from the same cDNA library that are non-homologous and lack a disclosed common property do not satisfy unity. The sugar-phosphate backbone is not a 'significant structural element.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Common property alone may be insufficient if structural elements are unrelated or prior art teaches the property
rubrics_metrics.description: A shared property (e.g., generating an antibody response) does not establish unity if (1) the structural elements that impart the property do not share a significant structural element, (2) any common structure does not impart the property, or (3) the property/combination is already known in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fusion protein example: carrier protein X is known and does not itself impart the property; small epitopes (SEQ ID NOs) do not share significant structure -> no unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: If common matter is known, remaining differing features must share a unifying novel inventive concept (a posteriori lack of unity)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the common matter linking claims is known from prior art, and the remaining subject-matter of each claim differs without a unifying novel inventive concept, lack of unity (a posteriori) exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humidifier example: if features of independent claim 1 are known, and claims 2 and 3 define substantially different technical aspects, these lack unity. The Guidelines caution that each case is considered on its merits and benefit of any doubt is given to the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims that add substantial divergent features can cause lack of unity a posteriori
rubrics_metrics.description: Dependent claims that introduce substantial features diverging from the inventive concept of the independent claim may be considered separate inventions if the independent claimed common matter is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: humidifier dependent claims 2 and 3 each define distinct inventive features (resistive wire + insulating layer vs. tubular support with wicking) that are not linked by a single inventive concept once common matter is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single independent claim can contain multiple inventions (lack of unity within one claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single independent claim that defines alternatives by steps or features may lack unity if the common feature is known and the alternative steps provide unrelated technical contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orthotic formation example: the common template preparation may be known; claims splitting into (attach upper layer) vs (heating template) could be separate inventions if common matter is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex/overlapping claim sets: identify special technical features and group accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims overlap in features, examiners should identify the special technical feature(s) of each independent claim to determine whether a single general inventive concept links them; avoid narrow, literal, or academic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turbine blade/alloy example: independent claims directed to the blade shape and to alloy Z lack unity a priori if no special technical feature is common; but groupings may change depending on novelty/inventiveness findings (e.g., if blade is novel, unity exists between blade and dependent claim 2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum reasoning required when raising a non-unity objection
rubrics_metrics.description: When an Authority raises a non-unity objection it must provide minimum reasoning explaining why no technical relationship exists: identify the common matter and explain why it cannot provide a single general inventive concept, and why remaining features are not corresponding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (system with radiation detector vs drone; SNPs; surgical light): reasoning should state that the common matter is known from prior art (so not a special technical feature) and explain the differing technical properties/functions of the remaining features (e.g., radiation detector detects nuclear threat vs drone improves signal/noise).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of the common matter linking the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiners should explicitly identify the common matter linking the subject-matter of the claims and use that to analyze whether a same or corresponding special technical feature exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance examples show stepwise identification: state the common features (e.g., method of diagnosing disease X by genotyping at least one of SNPs) and then analyze whether that common matter is known and whether the alternatives add corresponding special technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaches for selecting the 'first invention' in large-variable claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When a broad formula with many variables lacks a readily ascertainable significant structural element, examiners may determine a 'first invention' by (a) considering the content of dependent claims, (b) taking the first-mentioned structure for each variable, or (c) selecting a broader first invention as some Authorities do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different Authorities may adopt different approaches; dependent claims limited to the first invention may be searched without additional fees; other combinations may be invited for additional search fees. Description and examples can guide selection of useful groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological claims: 'isolated' term and Office practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Authorities presume biological molecules are claimed in isolated form and do not require the explicit term 'isolated'; others require explicit wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply local/Authority-specific practice when assessing claims to polynucleotides, proteins, SNPs, fusion proteins, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: SNP and point-mutation claims: need disclosed common property or functional relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims listing single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) or point mutations in a sequence lack unity if the mutations are uncharacterized and no common property or activity is disclosed; presence within the same prior-known sequence is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: SNPs within SEQ ID NO:1 where SEQ ID NO:1 is prior art and no function is identified -> lack of unity. Groupings proposed: treat each SNP as separate invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure after deciding lack of unity at international search stage: invitation to pay additional fees
rubrics_metrics.description: When lack of unity is decided (except in specified circumstances), the International Searching Authority issues a communication (invitation to pay additional fees) specifying reasons for non-unity and identifying the separate inventions and number of additional search fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form PCT/ISA/206 is used; the invitation normally precedes the international search report and written opinion, except as noted in related paragraphs.
